Congress’s power to determine who appoints those individuals who 
work for the federal government turns on the Appointments Clause in 
Article II. That clause provides that the President:
shall nominate, and by and with the advice and consent of the 
Senate, shall appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and 
consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other officers of the 
United States, whose appointments are not herein otherwise 
provided for, and which shall be established by law: but the 
Congress may by law vest the appointment of such inferior 
officers, as they think proper, in the President alone, in the courts 
of law, or in the heads of departments.
U.S. Co n s t ., art. II, K 2. The text thus enumerates four methods of 
appointment. The default process—and the only possibility for officers 
other than “inferior officers”—^is presidential appointment with Senate 
advice and consent. As to inferior officers. Congress may choose that option, 
as weU, but it may also permit appointment by “the President alone, 
“courts of law,” or “heads of departments.” As a threshold matter, however, 
Congress is hmited to these four possibilities only if the individual working 
for the governmAnt is an “officer[ ] of the United States, not someone 
working in some other capacity, which case law calls employee. This 
section addresses both the distinction between officer and employee and 
the hne between principal and inferior status.
